strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in differentiable optimization layers: avoiding KKT-system factorization and Hessian-based implicit differentiation during the backward pass.

The active-set ghost reformulation is an interesting idea: locally convert active inequalities into equality constraints and use a perturbed lower-level solve to approximate the hypergradient with first-order quantities.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering QP-style decision-focused learning, Sudoku, and SOCP, with comparisons to CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, and dQP.
The implementation goal is practically appealing. A solver-agnostic layer compatible with CVXPY-style modeling would be useful if robustly reproducible.
The paper includes some discussion of the active-set requirement and provides ablations on memory, problem dimension, batch size, solver tolerance, and gradient similarity.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantees depend on strong and partly unrealistic assumptions: exact active-set identification, LICQ, local active-set constancy, strong regularity, and strong convexity of the lower-level objective. These assumptions exclude many of the regimes where differentiable optimization layers are difficult in practice, especially near active-set changes.

The extension to general convex constraints is not fully convincing. It introduces an oracle that returns approximate primal-dual solutions with the same active set, bounded pseudoinverse, bounded duals, and other regularity assumptions; the final corollary is largely argued by analogy rather than a complete complexity proof.

The claim of being 'fully first-order' is somewhat overstated. The method avoids differentiating through KKT systems, but it still requires solving original and perturbed constrained optimization problems and obtaining reliable dual variables/active sets; in experiments and discussion it invokes sophisticated solvers, not purely first-order training primitives.

The hypergradient estimator is only locally valid and can fail near weakly active constraints or active-set transitions. The paper acknowledges this but the experiments do not stress-test such cases, so the practical robustness of the central approximation remains uncertain.

The experimental reporting is mostly qualitative through plots, with limited numerical tables, no visible confidence intervals despite 10 seeds, and incomplete hyperparameter/data-generation details in the main text. Baseline fairness is hard to assess, especially for LPGD tolerance choices and the self-implemented BPQP baseline.

Reproducibility is inadequate for an ICML main-track acceptance-level claim: the abstract says source code is available but no link is provided, and key implementation details for active-set detection, dual recovery, solver tolerances, and perturbed-problem construction are underspecified.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence: inconsistent naming between FFOLayer/FFOCP/FFOQP, typos such as 'well-clock time' and memory units, and a memory figure described as GPU memory despite CPU-only experiments.

The impact/ethics discussion is very brief. This is not a major ethical concern, but the paper could better discuss failure modes when embedded optimization layers are used in high-stakes decision systems with misspecified constraints.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in differentiable optimization layers: avoiding costly KKT/Hessian-based backward passes while retaining compatibility with standard convex solvers.

The active-set/ghost-problem viewpoint is a potentially useful conceptual connection between differentiable optimization layers and first-order bilevel methods, and the paper attempts to provide finite-time hypergradient and stationarity guarantees rather than only an empirical heuristic.

The experimental section compares against several relevant baselines, including CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, and dQP, and includes runtime, memory, scaling, tolerance, batch-size, and gradient-similarity ablations.
The manuscript is mostly readable at a high level and contains appendices that try to spell out proof details and discuss why exact active-set identification is a nontrivial requirement.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claims rely on very strong and partly unrealistic assumptions. Exact active-set identification is assumed in the main theorem, and for general convex constraints the paper assumes an oracle that returns approximate primal-dual solutions with the same active set. This substantially weakens the practical meaning of the claimed O(log(1/epsilon)) hypergradient oracle and the solver-agnostic guarantee.

The paper’s 'fully first-order' framing is overstated. The analysis requires twice differentiability, Hessian smoothness, strong regularity of KKT systems, LICQ, strong convexity, bounded dual/primal quantities, and dual recovery. The algorithm also depends on multipliers and active constraints from the solver, which are precisely delicate quantities in ill-conditioned constrained problems.

Several proof steps are under-justified. The active-set equivalence proof assumes away weakly active constraints and local active-set changes; strict complementarity/local constancy are not cleanly formalized. The general convex-constraint extension is especially thin: after deriving closeness lemmas, Corollary D.5 essentially asserts the same rate follows. Theorem C.2 also states \tilde O(1) oracle evaluations while the main text claims O(log(1/epsilon)), creating ambiguity about what is being counted.

The empirical evidence does not convincingly validate the central claims. The tasks are synthetic or toy-like, with no real decision-focused/control/meta-learning benchmark where solver-agnostic deployment matters. Convergence is measured mainly by training loss rather than downstream/test performance, and the gradient comparison uses CvxpyLayer as a proxy rather than a true exact oracle.

Runtime comparisons raise fairness concerns. Some baselines are official but BPQP is reimplemented by the authors; methods use different solver backends; most results are CPU-only despite QPTH being GPU-capable; and the paper attributes advantages to first-order differentiation even when forward canonicalization/solver choices appear to dominate. Claims such as sublinear scaling from wall-clock plots are not established theoretically or statistically.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says source code is available but the link is blank. Appendix G gives only coarse details and omits many exact hyperparameters, solver versions/settings, hardware details beyond allocation, and enough implementation detail to reproduce active-set handling and perturbed solves.

Presentation has many signs of insufficient polishing: duplicated references, malformed text such as '10=12', 'well-clock', 'Memory Usage (GD)', repeated 'Lemma Lemma', inconsistent theorem names/rates, and vague statements such as 'sufficient number of epochs'. These issues make it harder to trust the technical care of the submission.

The limitations and ethics discussion is minimal. The paper acknowledges active-set issues in an appendix, but the main narrative continues to sell broad solver-agnostic scalability. Risks from incorrect gradients under active-set ambiguity, weak complementarity, solver tolerances, and approximate duals are not adequately reflected in the claims.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in differentiable optimization layers: avoiding Hessian/KKT-system differentiation while retaining useful finite-time guarantees. The proposed active-set/ghost bilevel reformulation is a promising and technically interesting way to reduce inequality-constrained layers to equality-constrained first-order hypergradient estimation locally.

The contribution is well positioned relative to CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, and dQP. The solver-agnostic implementation idea is practically valuable, especially the reduction of the perturbed backward solve to adding a linear term from the incoming gradient signal.

The theory is meaningful: under LICQ, strong convexity, correct active-set identification, and regularity assumptions, the paper argues for epsilon-accurate approximate hypergradients with near-constant/logarithmic overhead and for an overall Goldstein-stationarity complexity matching known nonsmooth nonconvex rates. The appendix also discusses why active-set information is intrinsically difficult and provides a smoothed alternative without the same requirement.

The experiments cover several relevant settings, including synthetic decision-focused QPs, a Sudoku-style LP/QP task, and SOCPs with nonlinear convex constraints. The comparisons include strong baselines and useful ablations on problem dimension, memory, LPGD tolerance, gradient similarity, batch size, and solver tolerance.

Empirical results support the central practical claim: FFOLayer obtains convergence similar to exact or KKT-based layers while often improving backward/runtime and memory scaling, especially in larger or ill-conditioned problems.
weaknesses: The main guarantees rely on strong assumptions that substantially limit scope: strongly convex lower-level objectives, LICQ, locally constant/correctly identified active sets, differentiability of the hyper-objective, and strong regularity. These are reasonable for some convex layers but exclude many common degenerate or weakly active regimes where differentiable optimization layers are difficult in practice.

The general convex-constraint extension is less satisfying than the linear case because it assumes access to an approximate primal-dual oracle with the same active constraints and bounded pseudoinverses/dual norms. This makes the claimed extension to general convex constraints somewhat conditional and less algorithmically complete.

Some proof and presentation details need tightening. For example, Theorem C.2 states a tilde-O(1) oracle bound while the main theorem states O(log(1/epsilon)); the finite-difference formula and subsequent derivation are somewhat notation-heavy and appear inconsistent in places about whether the constraint term is evaluated at y* or y_delta. These issues do not invalidate the idea, but they make the technical argument harder to audit.

The empirical evaluation is convincing for scalability but mostly synthetic or stylized. A real decision-focused/control/structured-prediction benchmark would strengthen the significance claim, especially since solver-agnosticism is presented as a practical advantage.

Runtime results are mostly communicated through plots without detailed numeric tables, uncertainty intervals, or statistical variability despite using 10 seeds. Some baseline choices also need more justification, such as excluding Alt-Diff from main results and using tightened LPGD tolerances that may differ from prior work.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper says the source code is available, but the URL appears blank in the manuscript, and exact hyperparameters are described only at a high level. Providing the repository, scripts, solver versions, and tabulated settings would be important for others to build on the work.

The limitations discussion is present but brief. The paper would benefit from a clearer main-text discussion of failure modes: active-set misidentification, non-strict complementarity, noisy/inaccurate solvers, nondifferentiable optima, and how the method behaves when lower-level strong convexity is weak.
